prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels, bringing frequency standards to the 1e-18 level.

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange my preferred configuration is unchanged: B042 alone, credited to Katori and Ye. Nothing in the eight statements weakened the case, and the chair's summary shows that all eight members regard it as mature, reproducible and cleanly attributed, with five preferring it and the other three listing it as an alternative. I do not rest on that count. The scientific point is that the magic-wavelength condition removes the light shift that would otherwise forbid trapping the atoms, so thousands of atoms can be interrogated at once in a regime free of Doppler and recoil broadening. That is what gives the stability that makes 1e-18 accuracy reachable in practice, and it is a separable idea from the optical frequency comb honoured in 2005 and from the single-ion control honoured in 2012. The results have been reproduced and compared between independent laboratories, and the uses, tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the roadmap for the second, are already concrete. A two-name credit maps onto an identifiable concept with its first demonstration and the record performance. As I said publicly, the prize is for a discovery or invention rather than a lifetime of work (as reported by Tohoku University), and this is an invention that did something its predecessors could not. I would ask that the citation name the magic-wavelength lattice and its realisation, and not frequency metrology in general.
statement.case_against: The reservations that remain are real and I have not argued them away. First, overlap: the 2005 and 2012 prizes surround this territory, and Ye's comb and ultrastable-laser work sits close to the first. The citation must therefore be narrow, and the committee must be willing to say that the many-atom lattice scheme is the new step. Second, attribution: Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and other groups made real contributions, and no member, including me, has verified the early-proposal record against the documents. If that record showed priority that two names cannot honour, I would want to reconsider. Third, the SI second has not yet been redefined, so some of the practical culmination is prospective, though I regard that as a policy step and not a scientific test. Finally, the instrument-and-method character of the work is, from my own microscopy background, something I am sensitive to in both directions: I would not want to apply a stricter standard to a clock than I would apply to an electron microscope.

responses.point: The chair asks Kroll whether the stability gained from interrogating many atoms at once is the decisive point of separation from the 2005 comb prize; Kroll argues the lattice-clock concept is a separable original step and admits he has not checked current best uncertainties or other early contributors.
responses.response: I would answer the chair's question as an experimentalist and say yes. A single trapped ion gives excellent accuracy but a small signal, so averaging time is long; the lattice trades that for a very large atom number with the perturbation engineered to cancel. The decisive step is the combination of tight confinement without a clock shift and a large atom number, and that is not in the comb or the ion-control prizes. I would hold the citation to that, and I still agree with you that neither of us can certify the early-proposal record from memory.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, supports B042 with a narrow citation anchored on the neutral-atom magic-wavelength scheme and flags that Ye's comb and ultrastable-laser work sits partly in 2005 territory, and that he relies on memory for the priority history of Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and Takamoto.
responses.response: I agree that the citation has to be written narrowly, and I would go one step further than you did: it should not mention ultrastable lasers or combs at all, so that Ye is credited for taking the lattice clock to record accuracy and stability, not for the enabling toolbox. That keeps the 2005 boundary visible in the text. On priority I share your reliance on memory. I would want the secretariat to put the dated first proposal and the first demonstrations in front of us before the vote, and I would count a clear priority problem against two names, not merely note it.

responses.point: Danielsson, whose own first choice was the Higgs discovery, now supports B042 as the case with clean attribution, and says B057 is the plainest discovery on the list but a policy choice about crediting collaboration leadership.
responses.response: I appreciate that you put your own first choice second to the attribution test, and I take your policy point seriously. My view is that the committee should not adopt a collaboration-credit convention in the same sitting in which it is trying to decide a prize, so B057 should stay my second alternative and not enter the preferred configuration this year. If the committee does want to settle that convention, then the citation would have to say plainly that it honours detector concepts and leadership, and I would want to hear you word it before judging.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers magic-angle graphene, argues that waiting a few years is not costless, that the criterion is the discovery and not a closed theory of its origin, and names B042 as his fallback.
responses.response: The superconductivity comparison is fair, and I have moved a little: I accept that an open pairing mechanism does not by itself disqualify a discovery. My remaining concern is narrower and comes from my own experience with oxide interfaces, where properties depend on sample-to-sample structure. In B019 the dependence on twist-angle disorder and sample quality is exactly that kind of issue, and the omitted junior experimentalists who led the first papers make the credit harder to fix. I would keep B019 as my first alternative and would not oppose it if it is the committee's choice in a later year, but I do not think waiting costs the field anything comparable to the clarity B042 offers now.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B038 but concedes that the 2012 overlap, the Wineland and Monroe claims and the bundling with cold-atom simulation make B042 the cleaner attribution, and he discloses his superconducting-circuit interests at Chalmers.
responses.response: I thank you again for the disclosure, and as I said, being colleagues at Chalmers I will treat your assessment of the circuit and ion platforms with that in mind and ask the committee to weigh mine the same way. Your own answer to the chair, that B038 would have to be scoped to the gate proposal and its realisation, does not remove the problem for me, because even narrowly scoped it leaves Wineland and Monroe on the record as the first ion gate. I could not support B038 in the preferred configuration unless that boundary were settled by documents, but I accept that it deserves a fuller discussion in a future year.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers dynamical mean-field theory, lists B042 as an alternative, and considers whether the unreached redefinition of the second is a reason to wait.
responses.response: On the redefinition I disagree gently: the committee judges the discovery, and the reproduced 1e-18 comparisons are the evidence, whereas the redefinition is a decision by metrologists that follows from them. On B033 I read your reply to the chair as honest, and I stay where I was: a three-name DMFT configuration that omits Metzner for the infinite-dimension step is difficult to defend, and I do not see how the concept and the impurity mapping could be cited without it. That is a judgement about attribution, not about the importance of the framework, and I would support keeping it on the list.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B042 first, asks that the citation state the boundary with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes explicitly, and flags the need to check shared-publication links for any other credited names.
responses.response: I agree with your request for an explicit boundary, and I think the wording I give in my citation does that, by naming the magic-wavelength trapping and the cancellation of the light shift. Since you work in the same atomic-physics community as Katori and Ye, I take your statement that none of your links involve them as sufficient for B042, as I would hope colleagues take mine about Japan. If the committee wants a further check, it should be applied evenly, to both of us and to Kroll's Hall connection.

uncertainties: The dated first proposal and first demonstration of the lattice clock have not been verified by any member, so priority among Katori, Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and others remains an open question that could affect two-name credit.

Whether the committee accepts that the many-atom, light-shift-free lattice scheme is separable from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control recognition, and whether Ye's comb-related work can be left out of the citation.
Whether the pending SI redefinition should delay recognition; I think not, but I cannot exclude that some colleagues will weigh it differently.
Whether the pairing mechanism and sample dependence in magic-angle graphene will settle soon enough to change the maturity judgement for B019 in future years.
Whether the committee adopts any convention for crediting collaborations, which would change the standing of B057 as an alternative.
statement.conflict_note: I remain recused from deliberating on B028 (aberration-corrected electron microscopy), which is in my own research field and where I led the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy; it is not part of my preferred configuration and I do not list it among my alternatives. I record my University of Tokyo and JSPS fellowships and exchanges with Japanese universities for B042, because Katori is at a Japanese institution, with no documented personal or collaborative tie to Katori or Ye. I am at Chalmers together with Goran Johansson, who has interests in B049 and B038, so I do not treat his assessment of those as independent. I have no direct tie to B019 or B057 beyond general familiarity with the field.
